plan.chapterName: OpenStax Calculus, chapter 12: Vectors in Space
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a three-dimensional coordinate plot showing two vectors in standard position together with both of their cross products. The axes are thin black lines carrying evenly spaced tick marks: a vertical one labeled z, one descending to the lower right labeled y, and one descending to the lower left labeled x. Two short orange arrows leave the origin, one pointing to the right and labeled u = <0, 2, 1>, the other pointing down and to the left and labeled v = <3, -1, 0>. A long red arrow runs from the origin downward and to the right, reaching the bottom of the frame, labeled u x v = <1, 3, -6>. A long teal arrow runs from the origin upward and slightly to the left, reaching the top of the frame, labeled v x u = <-1, -3, 6>. Each long arrow is wrapped in a dashed blue rectangular box whose edges project its tip back onto the coordinate directions, making the endpoint coordinates readable. Drawing both products from a common origin makes it plain that they lie along a single line but point in opposite senses, each standing perpendicular to the plane spanned by u and v. The plot supports the relation u x v = -(v x u).

demo_steps.title: Vectors in standard position
demo_steps.narration: The two orange vectors start at the origin: u points mostly along positive y with a small positive z component, while v lies in the xy-plane. Their cross products lie on one shared line through the origin.

demo_steps.title: Order u × v
demo_steps.narration: With u × v selected, the red arrow is the active result and points to ⟨1, 3, −6⟩. The dashed box projects that endpoint back along the coordinate directions.

demo_steps.title: Reverse the order
demo_steps.narration: Switching to v × u activates the teal arrow, which points exactly opposite the red arrow. Its endpoint ⟨−1, −3, 6⟩ is the sign reversal of ⟨1, 3, −6⟩.

demo_steps.title: Right-hand rule result
demo_steps.narration: Step through the rule: fingers align with u, curl toward v, and the thumb points along the red u × v direction. This connects the geometric hand rule to the downward red result vector.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use mathematical world coordinates directly: u = (0, 2, 1), v = (3, −1, 0), u × v = (1, 3, −6), v × u = (−1, −3, 6). Axis span should cover approximately x ∈ [−4, 4], y ∈ [−4, 4], z ∈ [−7, 7], with tick marks every 1 unit. Match the source orientation: +Z appears vertical upward on screen, +Y recedes down-right, and +X recedes down-left. The red u × v arrow points downward and right in the rendered view; the teal v × u arrow points upward and slightly left along the same line. Draw dashed coordinate guide boxes as axis-aligned wireframe boxes whose opposite corners are the origin and the cross-product endpoint: one box from (0,0,0) to (1,3,−6), and one from (0,0,0) to (−1,−3,6). Dominant colors: axes and labels black #111111; u and v orange #ff6a1a; u × v red #e53935; v × u teal #159c9c; dashed guide boxes dark blue #005a9c. Vectors should use cylindrical shafts about 0.035 units radius with cone arrowheads about 0.18 units long; cross-product arrows should be slightly thicker than the orange input vectors.
interactionPlan.notes: Use an orthographic/axonometric camera, not perspective convergence. Use dashed LineSegments or LineDashedMaterial for the blue guide boxes, with dash and gap lengths scaled consistently in world units. Keep both cross-product arrows visible to preserve the source figure, but the product-order toggle should make the selected arrow fully opaque and its label bold while dimming the opposite arrow to about 25–35% opacity. The right-hand-rule button should reveal overlays progressively: first highlight u, then add a curved arrow in the plane from u toward v, then brighten the red u × v result arrow and show a small thumb-direction marker. Use CSS2D or sprite text labels that face the camera while staying anchored near their corresponding vectors.

authoredContext:
We see that, in this case, u×v=−(v×u) (the figure). We prove this in general later in this section.

The cross products u×v and v×u are both orthogonal to u and v, but in opposite directions.

This figure is the 3-dimensional coordinate system. It has two vectors in standard position. The first vector is labeled “u = <0, 2, 1>.” The second vector is labeled “v = <3, -1, 0>.” It also has two vectors that are cross products. The first is “u x v = <1, 3, -6>.” The second is “v x u = <-1, -3, 6>.”
